finding: The male triage row treats elevated PVR and an enlarged prostate as sufficient to direct outlet treatment, despite the page's warning about detrusor underactivity.
evidence: EAU 2026 male LUTS diagnostic guideline, https://uroweb.org/guidelines/management-of-non-neurogenic-male-luts/chapter/diagnostic-evaluation: high PVR can reflect obstruction and/or poor detrusor function; no PVR treatment threshold is established.

edit.old: | High voiding score, enlarged prostate, elevated PVR | Treat outlet obstruction first or concurrently |
edit.new: | High voiding score, enlarged prostate, elevated PVR | Assess for both outlet obstruction and detrusor underactivity before selecting outlet treatment; PVR and prostate size alone do not establish obstruction.<sup>[[24]](#ref24)</sup> |

finding: FUTURE's 23.6% versus 22.7% are outcome-evaluable fractions, not rates among all 1,099 analyzed women; the page does not define success or specify the final follow-up interval.
evidence: NIHR FUTURE primary report, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK615958/pdf/Bookshelf_NBK615958.pdf, Table 5: PGI-I 'much improved' or 'very much improved' at last follow-up (15 or 24 months) was 117/496 versus 114/503; adjusted OR 1.12 (95% CI 0.73–1.74).

edit.old: At final follow-up, patient-reported success was 23.6% versus 22.7% (adjusted OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.73–1.74); adding urodynamics did not demonstrate superiority.
edit.new: At 15- or 24-month final follow-up, 117/496 women (23.6%) assigned urodynamics plus clinical assessment and 114/503 (22.7%) assigned clinical assessment alone rated their bladder symptoms 'much improved' or 'very much improved' (adjusted OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.73–1.74); adding urodynamics did not demonstrate superiority.

finding: The 53% augmentation result is complete continence, not general symptomatic success, and 27 of 51 women had associated interstitial cystitis; the cross-cohort wording overstates a general difference.
evidence: Awad et al., PMID 9598629, DOI 10.1046/j.1464-410x.1998.00549.x, publisher abstract https://bjui-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1464-410x.1998.00549.x: 27/51 completely continent, 13/51 occasional leaks, 20/51 regular CIC, mean 75.4 months; 27 had interstitial cystitis.

edit.old: Older cohort data suggest augmentation results are markedly worse in idiopathic OAB than in neuropathic bladder disease: long-term symptomatic success as low as about 53% in an idiopathic-urge-incontinence cohort, versus the substantially higher success reported in neuropathic cohorts, with revision of the augmentation reported in a wide range (roughly 5–40%) across series and metabolic acidosis requiring bicarbonate in a minority.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)[[16]](#ref16)</sup>
edit.new: One 51-woman non-neurogenic UUI series (27 with associated interstitial cystitis) reported complete continence in 27/51 (53%), occasional leaks in 13/51 (25%), and regular self-catheterization in 20/51 (39%) at a mean 75.4 months. Across augmentation series, revision has been reported in a wide range (roughly 5–40%), and a minority required bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis.<sup>[[15]](#ref15)[[16]](#ref16)</sup>

finding: The cited ileal-conduit complication series enrolled only neurologically impaired patients, so it cannot establish an OAB-specific complication rate.
evidence: Chartier-Kastler et al., PMID 12185605, DOI 10.1038/sj.sc.3101346, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12185605/: 33 neurogenic-bladder patients, 12/33 with perioperative complications, 4/19 bladder-retaining patients with pyocystitis, mean 48-month follow-up. EAU 2026 https://uroweb.org/guidelines/non-neurogenic-female-luts/chapter/disease-management says no studies specifically examined diversion techniques for intractable OAB/UUI.

edit.old: Ileal conduit diversion for OAB has also been reported to carry a substantial complication rate over time and is reserved for the most extreme situations.<sup>[[17]](#ref17)</sup>
edit.new: For idiopathic OAB/UUI, the EAU 2026 guideline reserves diversion for patients who have failed less invasive therapy, accept a stoma, and understand malignancy risk (Weak). In a separate 33-patient neurogenic-bladder ileal-conduit series, 12/33 had a perioperative complication and 4/19 who retained the bladder developed pyocystitis at mean 48-month follow-up.<sup>[[13]](#ref13)[[17]](#ref17)</sup>

finding: Major-surgery counseling omits the ability to perform intermittent catheterization after augmentation and the need for lifelong surveillance.
evidence: EAU 2026 female LUTS guideline, https://uroweb.org/guidelines/non-neurogenic-female-luts/chapter/disease-management: Strong recommendations to explain high IC risk, confirm willingness and ability to catheterize, provide lifelong surveillance and specialist-nurse support.

edit.old: In those patients, OAB/UUI should be reframed as a safe-storage problem, not merely a symptom-control problem.
edit.new: In those patients, OAB/UUI becomes a safe-storage problem. Before augmentation, assess willingness and ability to perform intermittent catheterization and counsel about lifelong surveillance; before diversion, discuss stoma acceptance and long-term complications.<sup>[[13]](#ref13)</sup>

finding: The claim that mirabegron has the strongest male evidence omits COURAGE, a 2024 placebo-controlled vibegron add-on trial in 1,105 men on BPH medication, and conflicts with the linked treatment database's vibegron option.
evidence: Staskin et al., COURAGE, J Urol 2024;212:256-266, DOI 10.1097/JU.0000000000003999, PubMed indexed abstract https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38708869/ (direct landing blocked); opened EAU 2026 male LUTS guideline https://uroweb.org/guidelines/management-of-non-neurogenic-male-luts/chapter/disease-management and opened GEMTESA label https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=25f21d25-14f8-4fda-91f6-7aa8b68aa1c8: 1,105 randomized to vibegron 75 mg or placebo for 24 weeks on alpha-blocker ±5ARI; week-12 urgency difference -0.95/day (95% CI -1.37 to -0.54); EAU add-on recommendation Weak and long-term evidence limited.

edit.old: In men, mirabegron has the strongest data beyond antimuscarinics.<sup>[[6]](#ref6)</sup>
edit.new: In men with persistent OAB symptoms despite BPH medication, the 2024 COURAGE trial randomized 1,105 men to vibegron 75 mg or placebo for 24 weeks and found 0.95 fewer daily urgency episodes with vibegron than placebo at week 12 (95% CI 0.54–1.37 fewer). The EAU 2026 male LUTS guideline weakly recommends a β3 agonist with an α-blocker for persistent storage symptoms and notes that add-on benefits are modest and longer-term evidence is limited.<sup>[[24]](#ref24)[[25]](#ref25)</sup>

finding: The mirabegron caution omits the label's explicit severe-uncontrolled-hypertension threshold and periodic BP monitoring.
evidence: MYRBETRIQ adult prescribing information section 5.1, https://www.dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=ba9e9e15-e666-4c56-9271-2e24739cfa2d: periodically check BP; mirabegron is not recommended with SBP ≥180 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥110 mm Hg.

edit.old: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure; check interactions and baseline hypertension
edit.new: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure; monitor BP periodically, check interactions, and note that it is not recommended with SBP ≥180 mm Hg or DBP ≥110 mm Hg.<sup>[[26]](#ref26)</sup>

finding: PTNS and surface-electrode TTNS are combined as one minimally invasive procedure with one schedule, although the guideline classifies TTNS as noninvasive and its optimal regimen is unsettled.
evidence: AUA/SUFU 2024 guideline Table 1, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/nau.25532: TTNS is noninvasive; PTNS is minimally invasive. EAU 2026 female LUTS https://uroweb.org/guidelines/non-neurogenic-female-luts/chapter/disease-management: TTNS uses surface electrodes and its optimal schedule is not established.

edit.old: | [**PTNS / TTNS**](/docs/surgical-techniques/04f-incontinence-procedures/procedures/percutaneous-tibial-nerve-stimulation) | Patient preferring low-risk office or home neuromodulation | Weekly induction and maintenance; low systemic adverse-effect burden |
edit.new:
| [**PTNS**](/docs/surgical-techniques/04f-incontinence-procedures/procedures/percutaneous-tibial-nerve-stimulation) | Patient preferring office neuromodulation | Weekly office induction followed by maintenance; low systemic adverse-effect burden |
| **TTNS** | Patient preferring noninvasive surface-electrode stimulation | Optimal schedule is not established; discuss the separate evidence base and treatment burden.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[13]](#ref13)</sup> |

finding: The heading classifies all listed treatments as minimally invasive even though the table includes noninvasive TTNS.
evidence: AUA/SUFU 2024 guideline Table 1, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/nau.25532 distinguishes noninvasive TTNS from minimally invasive PTNS, botulinum toxin and SNM.

edit.old: ### Minimally invasive therapy
edit.new: ### Noninvasive and minimally invasive therapy

finding: The vaginal-estrogen row applies the Expert Opinion strength for GSM with OAB to its separate recurrent-UTI prevention claim.
evidence: AUA/SUFU/AUGS GSM guideline 2025, https://www.auanet.org/documents/Guidelines/PDF/2025%20Guidelines/GSM%20Unabridged%202025.pdf, statements 12 and 13: OAB comorbidity is Expert Opinion; recurrent-UTI prevention is Moderate Recommendation, Grade B.

edit.old: Vaginal estrogen can improve local urinary symptoms and reduce recurrent UTI risk (AUA/SUFU/AUGS 2025: an option for GSM with comorbid OAB, Expert Opinion)
edit.new: For GSM with comorbid OAB, local low-dose vaginal estrogen may be offered to improve genitourinary symptoms (Expert Opinion); for GSM with recurrent UTI, it is recommended to reduce future UTI risk (Moderate Recommendation, Grade B)

finding: The pharmacotherapy table repeats the GSM guideline-strength conflation for OAB and recurrent-UTI prevention.
evidence: AUA/SUFU/AUGS GSM guideline 2025, https://www.auanet.org/documents/Guidelines/PDF/2025%20Guidelines/GSM%20Unabridged%202025.pdf, statements 12 and 13: distinct Expert Opinion and Moderate/Grade B recommendations.

edit.old: Local therapy for GSM-associated urinary symptoms and recurrent UTI risk (AUA/SUFU/AUGS 2025 option, Expert Opinion)<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup>
edit.new: For GSM with OAB, local low-dose vaginal estrogen may be offered (Expert Opinion); for GSM with recurrent UTI, it is recommended to reduce future UTI risk (Moderate Recommendation, Grade B).<sup>[[14]](#ref14)</sup>

finding: The medication recommendation lacks the AUA/SUFU Strong/Grade A label.
evidence: AUA/SUFU 2024 guideline statement 16, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/nau.25532: antimuscarinic or β3 therapy is Strong Recommendation, Grade A.

edit.old: The AUA/SUFU guideline supports offering antimuscarinic medications or β3 agonists to patients with OAB, with shared decision-making around side effects and patient priorities.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup>
edit.new: The AUA/SUFU guideline recommends offering antimuscarinic medications or β3 agonists to patients with OAB (Strong Recommendation, Grade A), with shared decision-making around side effects and patient priorities.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup>

finding: The AUA/SUFU procedural recommendation lacks its Moderate/Grade A label.
evidence: AUA/SUFU 2024 guideline statement 25, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/nau.25532: offer SNM, tibial nerve stimulation and/or intradetrusor botulinum toxin after inadequate response or intolerable adverse effects (Moderate Recommendation, Grade A).

edit.old: It also recommends offering SNM, PTNS, and/or intradetrusor botulinum toxin after inadequate response or intolerable adverse effects from behavioral or drug treatment.
edit.new: It also recommends offering SNM, PTNS, and/or intradetrusor botulinum toxin after inadequate response or intolerable adverse effects from behavioral or drug treatment (Moderate Recommendation, Grade A).

finding: The behavioral paragraph omits the guideline's distinct Strong/Grade A bladder-training and Clinical Principle behavioral-therapy labels.
evidence: AUA/SUFU 2024 guideline statements 11-12, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/nau.25532.

edit.old: Offer bladder training and behavioral treatment to all patients; these can continue alongside medication or a procedure.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[7]](#ref7)</sup>
edit.new: Offer bladder training to all patients (AUA/SUFU 2024: Strong Recommendation, Grade A) and behavioral therapies to all patients (Clinical Principle); these can continue alongside medication or a procedure.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[7]](#ref7)</sup>

finding: The cited AUA/SUFU guideline does not substantiate the unqualified 'up to 40%' estimate across UUI patients; preserve the diagnostic teaching without that unsupported population estimate.
evidence: Opened AUA/SUFU 2024 full text, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/nau.25532, evaluation statements 5-6 and 29: no urodynamic finding confirms OAB and UDS is not required for diagnosis; it does not provide a 40% UUI estimate.

edit.old: Up to 40% of patients with urgency urinary incontinence do not have DO on urodynamics, so its absence in a patient with UUI or mixed incontinence does not exclude it as the causative mechanism; a normal urodynamic tracing should not be used to rule out OAB or UUI.
edit.new: DO can be absent on urodynamics in patients with UUI or mixed incontinence; a normal tracing does not rule out the clinical OAB/UUI syndrome.

finding: A case-control association in women is described as an independent risk factor, implying causality and a broader population than studied.
evidence: Arya et al., PMID 10862848, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10862848/: 131 women with detrusor instability and 128 controls, all with incontinence symptoms; caffeine >400 mg/day versus <100 mg/day was associated with OR 2.4 (95% CI 1.1–6.5) after adjustment; causality was not established.

edit.old: a case-control study found intake above 400 mg/day of caffeine an independent risk factor for detrusor instability (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.1–6.5) after controlling for age and smoking
edit.new: in a case-control study of 259 women with incontinence symptoms undergoing urodynamics, intake above 400 mg/day was associated with higher odds of detrusor instability than intake below 100 mg/day after adjustment for age and smoking (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.1–6.5); causality was not established

finding: The mouse PIEZO finding is broader than the observed sex- and activity-specific phenotype, and afferent coupling is proposed rather than directly established.
evidence: Dalghi et al., DOI 10.1172/jci.insight.152984, full text https://insight.jci.org/articles/view/152984: male urothelial Piezo2-knockout mice and both sexes with dual Piezo1/2 knockout leaked during the active dark phase; stretch and ATP responses were measured.

edit.old: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 channels act as bladder-stretch sensors that couple filling to afferent signaling; in knockout mice, loss of PIEZO2 (and combined PIEZO1/2 loss) produces incontinence
edit.new: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 participate in mouse urothelial responses to stretch and ATP release; male Piezo2-knockout mice and both sexes with dual Piezo1/2 knockout leaked during the active dark phase

finding: The microbiome row presents a fairly uniform dysbiosis pattern despite heterogeneous observational phenotypes and a small mirabegron cohort.
evidence: Zhou et al., DOI 10.3389/fcimb.2022.1030315, open full text https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cellular-and-infection-microbiology/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2022.1030315/full: 64 women receiving mirabegron; Shaker et al. 2025 open full text https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11857253/ describes variable patterns; EAU 2026 https://uroweb.org/guidelines/non-neurogenic-female-luts/chapter/diagnostic-evaluation advises against routine urinary microbiota assessment.

edit.old: reduced Lactobacillus dominance and increased microbial diversity correlate with symptom severity in urgency and mixed incontinence and with treatment response to mirabegron, distinct from infection-driven urgency and still an active research area rather than a diagnostic or treatment lever
edit.new: small studies in women associate urinary microbial composition with UUI severity; one 64-woman cohort found higher Lactobacillus abundance among mirabegron responders. Findings vary by phenotype and sampling method, and the EAU 2026 guideline recommends against routine microbiota assessment for diagnosis or management
